column1: Enhancing Inflation Nowcasting with LLM: Sentiment NEWS Index

The thesis titled Enhancing Inflation Nowcasting with LLM: Sentiment Analysis on News by Marc-Antoine Allard  Paul Teiletche  and Adam Zinebi from EPFL  Lausanne  investigates the integration of large language models (LLMs) into traditional inflation nowcasting frameworks  particularly during periods of high inflation volatility such as the COVID-19 pandemic. The authors introduce InflaBERT  a BERT-based LLM fine-tuned to predict inflation-related sentiment in news articles. This model is used to create NEWS  an index that captures the monthly sentiment of news regarding inflation. By incorporating this sentiment index into the Cleveland Fed’s model  which traditionally relies on macroeconomic autoregressive processes  the study demonstrates a marginal improvement in nowcast accuracy during the pandemic. This suggests the potential of combining sentiment analysis with traditional economic indicators  advocating for further research to refine these methodologies for better real-time inflation monitoring. The source code for this study is available on GitHub.

The introduction of the thesis highlights the significant economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic  which led to a surge in global inflation due to disruptions in supply chains  rising food prices  and increased inflation expectations. Inflation  defined as the annualized percent change in consumer prices  rose from 2% in 2019 to 8% in 2022  according to the World Bank. Although inflation has since receded  it remains higher than pre-pandemic levels. Controlling inflation is a primary objective for major central banks like the Federal Reserve  the European Central Bank  and the Swiss National Bank. In response to the inflation shock  these banks have significantly increased interest rates  impacting the economy  particularly the real estate sector. Monitoring real-time inflation dynamics is crucial for central banks  which have developed inflation nowcasting models. Nowcasting  a term originating in meteorology  refers to predicting the very recent past  present  and near future state of an economic indicator. Initially applied to economic growth  nowcasting models for inflation have recently been developed.

One popular model  developed by Knotek and Zaman  forms the basis of the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland's inflation nowcasting model. This model uses an Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression to forecast three main inflation components (core inflation  food prices  energy) based on autoregressive processes and high-frequency data like daily oil prices. The authors demonstrate that this nowcasting model outperforms forecasts by professional economists  as captured by the Survey of Professional Forecasters (SPF).

Recent advancements in machine learning and artificial intelligence have allowed nowcasting models to process a broader range of indicators than traditional economic statistics  including internet search trends  social media sentiment  and credit card transaction data. Examples include studies by Angelico et al.  de Bandt et al.  and Beck et al. The advent of Large Language Models (LLMs) offers an opportunity to enhance inflation nowcasting models  as shown by Faria e Castro and Leibovici with Google AI’s PaLM.

This project investigates whether these recent methodologies can improve traditional inflation nowcasting models. The authors model news inflation sentiment by introducing InflaBERT  a BERT-based LLM fine-tuned to predict inflation-related news sentiment. They train this model using an extensive news database from the FNSPID dataset. The authors propose NEWS  an index replicating monthly news sentiment regarding inflation  and test whether this index can improve the predictions of the Cleveland Fed nowcasting model. The focus is on the COVID period (2020-2023) to analyze how these models could have better tracked the strong moves and volatility in inflation during that time.

The related literature section of the thesis discusses the integration of AI in economic forecasting  specifically inflation prediction  as a burgeoning field leveraging advancements in machine learning and natural language processing. Recent studies  such as those by Faria-e-Castro and Leibovici  explore the potential of large language models (LLMs) like Google’s PaLM to generate accurate inflation forecasts. These studies demonstrate that LLMs can produce conditional inflation forecasts with lower mean-squared errors compared to traditional methods like the Survey of Professional Forecasters (SPF). The findings suggest that AI-based models can offer an effective and cost-efficient alternative to traditional expert and survey-based forecasting methods. This study aligns with previous works  such as those by Bybee  who used GPT-3.5 to simulate economic expectations  and extends the understanding of how LLMs can be utilized for macroeconomic and financial predictions.

column1: The section on news inflation sentiment analysis emphasizes the importance of incorporating population expectations into inflation nowcasting  given the strong correlation between human perceptions and realized inflation. Data from sources like Google Trends illustrate this phenomenon  showing increased searches for inflation during high inflation periods. Recognizing the valuable insights embedded in human behavior and perceptions  the authors chose news articles as their primary data source. News is comprehensive  highly relevant  and readily accessible  reflecting the opinions and signals that traders consider alongside mathematical models and prior information. This accessibility is a significant advantage compared to the costly acquisition of social data  such as Tweets.
